prompt: Let $A$ be a set and $R\subseteq A\times A$ a binary relation on $A$. For $x,y\in A$, write $R(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in R$. Which condition defines seriality?

answers.explanation: Each element has at least one outgoing related element, which may be itself.
Every element has a self-loop; pairs of different elements are unrestricted. This defines reflexivity, not seriality.
Every related pair has its reverse; loops are allowed but not required. This defines symmetry, not seriality.

answers.text: $\forall x\in A\;\forall y\in A\;\forall z\in A\; ((R(x,y)\land R(y,z))\Rightarrow R(x,z))$.
answers.explanation: Every two-step chain has its direct shortcut, including chains with repeated vertices. This defines transitivity, not seriality.
One related pair suffices; the other elements may be isolated. This defines nonemptiness, not seriality.

answers.text: $\forall x\in A\;\forall y\in A\;\forall z\in A\; ((R(x,y)\land R(x,z))\Rightarrow y=z)$.
answers.explanation: An element has at most one outgoing related element; it need not have any. This defines right-uniqueness, not seriality.

answers.text: $\forall x\in A\;\forall y\in A\; (x\ne y\Rightarrow (R(x,y)\lor R(y,x)))$.
answers.explanation: Every pair of distinct elements is comparable in at least one direction. This convention imposes no condition on loops. This defines connexity on distinct elements, not seriality.
Every element has a predecessor; this does not ensure that every element has a successor. This defines existence of an incoming neighbour for every element, not seriality.
One element must be a successor of every element; seriality can use different successors. This defines existence of one common outgoing target, not seriality.
Every ordered pair is present, including every loop. This defines universality, not seriality.
